**On Doorways, and the Things That Live in Them**

There's a phenomenon psychologists call the "doorway effect." You walk from the kitchen into the living room to get something, and by the time you arrive you've forgotten what it was. The leading explanation is that the brain treats a doorway as an event boundary. Crossing one tells your memory that a scene has ended, and it quietly files away what belonged to the previous room, including, unhelpfully, the errand. The doorway is not a neutral gap between spaces. It's a little machine for forgetting.

I find this oddly consoling. It means forgetfulness isn't always failure. Sometimes it's architecture doing its job. The house is constantly editing you.

I've been thinking about thresholds lately, in the loose way one thinks about things that have no deadline. The Romans had a god for them, Janus, who faced both directions at once, and they gave his name to the month in which the year turns over. In older houses the physical threshold was a raised sill, a literal plank you had to step over, and the word comes from "thresh," the act of beating grain, probably because the sill kept the loose straw of the floor from drifting out. So the word for the most symbolically loaded part of a house is, at root, a piece of agricultural housekeeping. This happens constantly with language. You pull on a grand abstraction and find a farmer's tool at the other end.

"Consider" is another one. It looks like it means simply to think carefully, but it's *con* plus *sidera*, "with the stars." To consider something was, originally, to consult the sky about it, to take an omen. When we ask someone to consider an offer, we are, etymologically, asking them to go outside at night and look up. Nobody means that anymore. But the fossil is still in the word, the way the shape of a shell is still in the limestone. I like knowing it's there. It doesn't change how I use the word, but it changes how the word feels in the hand.

Lichens are thresholds too, in their way, though not spatial ones. A lichen isn't a single organism. It's a fungus and an alga (or sometimes a cyanobacterium, or both) living so intimately that for a couple of centuries nobody realized it was a partnership at all. The fungus provides structure and holds water; the alga photosynthesizes and feeds them both. When Simon Schwendener proposed the dual nature of lichens in 1867, botanists were scandalized. It seemed a kind of category error, a violation of the tidy idea that every living thing was one thing. Beatrix Potter, before she wrote about rabbits in waistcoats, spent years peering at lichens through a microscope and was among those who took the idea seriously, though the scientific establishment had little interest in hearing it from her.

Now we know the story is even messier. Many lichens turn out to contain a third partner, a yeast, that went unnoticed until 2016. The thing that was supposed to be one organism, then two, might be three or more. And it grows on gravestones and tundra rock and the north side of trees at a pace that makes glaciers look hasty, sometimes a fraction of a millimeter a year. Some individual lichens are thought to be thousands of years old. They sit at the threshold between kingdoms of life and make a slow, crusty, orange-and-grey home there.

I think the reason these things gather together in my attention is that they're all examples of something being more than it advertises. The doorway that looks like an absence is actually doing cognitive work. The plain word carries a sky inside it. The grey scab on the rock is a household of strangers who have figured out how to be one body. None of this is visible from the surface, and the surface is fine on its own. You can live an entire life stepping through doorways, considering offers, and walking past lichens, and nothing is lost. But something is added if you look, and the addition costs almost nothing.

This is the case for the specific, I think, as against the general. General knowledge is useful, and I don't want to romanticize trivia. But the specific has a texture that the general lacks. "Language changes over time" is true and inert. "*Consider* means *with the stars*" is a small live thing you can pick up and carry around. It attaches to other things. It reminds you of the Romans who named the month, of the farmer beating grain, of Potter with her microscope in a century that didn't want to know what she'd seen. The specific is sticky. The general slides off.

There's a version of attention that feels like effort, the kind you summon for a spreadsheet or a difficult conversation. And there's another kind that feels more like permission. You let something small hold you for a moment longer than it strictly warrants. You stand in the doorway instead of passing through it. Nothing happens. Then you notice the sill, and the word, and the way the paint has worn where hands have touched the frame for forty years, and the doorway has become a place instead of a gap.

I don't have a conclusion, which seems appropriate for a piece about thresholds. Conclusions are doorways too, and I've just been arguing they make you forget. So let me end instead with the lichen, which has never concluded anything in ten thousand years and seems none the worse for it. It sits on its rock, three or four kinds of life pretending to be one, growing at a rate that renders the word "growing" almost ceremonial. It is not on its way anywhere. It has found a threshold and decided to live in it. That's a strange thing to admire, and I admire it anyway.
